grammar.title: Gramatyka
grammar.rule: Irena · z Ireną. Jan · z Janem. Z kim pracujesz? Pracuję z Ireną.
grammar.note_en:
The instrumental is a Polish noun case: a form that marks a word’s job in a sentence. Here it follows z and names a companion, the person with whom someone works or is present. Ewa jest z Ireną w warsztacie means “Ewa is with Irena in the workshop”. Ala pracuje z Ireną means “Ala works/is working with Irena”. Irena is not an object being taken or moved. She is Ala’s partner. Compare the naming form Irena with the companion form z Ireną. The preposition and ending work together; neither is an optional decoration.

For the feminine names here, change final -a to -ą: Irena → z Ireną, Ewa → z Ewą, Ala → z Alą. The feminine noun sąsiadka behaves similarly: sąsiadka → z sąsiadką. These mean “with Irena”, “with Ewa”, “with Ala” and “with a female neighbour”. Jan ends in a consonant: Jan → z Janem, “with Jan”. Przyjaciel → z przyjacielem means “with a friend”, referring to a male friend here. The table records these actual forms, not a promise that every Polish name or noun follows one identical pattern. Keep the ogonek (the small hook) in ą; Irena, Irenę and Ireną are different grammatical forms. This chapter teaches the naming and companion forms of the people, not personal direct objects.

Kto asks “who?” in a naming/subject question. Z kim asks “with whom?” or ordinary English “who … with?”. Kim is a form of the same question word, used here after z. Z kim pracujesz? means “Who do you work with?” Pracuję z Ireną means “I work with Irena”; the shorter reply Z Ireną is sufficient when the question supplies the activity. Do not use kto unchanged after z. Do not infer that kim is a general replacement for kto in every kind of question.

The present forms distinguish speaker and partner: pracuję means “I work/am working”, pracujesz “you work/are working”, and pracuje “works/is working”. Trzymam / trzymasz / trzyma means “I hold / you hold / holds”. Trzyma stół means “holds/steadies the table”; it describes an ongoing hold, whereas bierze stół would describe taking it. Ala trzyma stół and Irena obraca luźną nogę mean “Ala holds the table” and “Irena turns the loose leg”. The table remains upright and the leg stays attached. Trzyma takes the familiar affirmative object case: stół keeps its spelling, while noga becomes nogę. The companion phrase does not replace that object pattern.

Razem means “together”. Pracuje razem z Ireną means “works together with Irena”. The paired work supplies the meaning: one person holds the table while the other examines the loose leg, then they exchange tasks. Pomoc means “help/assistance”; Potrzebna jest pomoc means “Help is needed”. Potrzebna agrees with feminine pomoc; the earlier Potrzebny jest stolarz means “A carpenter is needed”. Rozmowa is a conversation: one person asks and the other answers, then their parts reverse. Przyjaciel names a friend, a social relationship. Sąsiad names a male neighbour, a relationship of living nearby. A person may be both, as Jan is here, but those words are not synonyms. The pictured friendship is not a claim that every neighbour is a friend.

Młotek is a hammer; wkręt is a screw. The hammer and screw are separated during preparation, not used to complete a repair. The loose table leg is still loose, and the lamp’s cable still has its crack. Pamiętam znak means “I remember the mark”. Irena’s recognition identifies the circle as familiar to her; it does not say who drew it, what it means or who owns the lamp.

This is a bounded use of the instrumental for accompaniment. Do not extend it here to saying that someone works by means of a hammer, to saying what someone’s occupation is, or to personal object pronouns. Naming To jest stolarz (“This is a carpenter”) is already possible; a noun predicate after a named subject is taught next chapter. The source meaning of z (“from/out of”) is later and uses a different case. Keep the present z kim and the demonstrated companion endings together.
